To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
TDH is a multifunctional toxin that triggers calcium-dependent chloride secretion in human and rat intestinal cell monolayers at concentrations that do not cause cell death.
V. parahaemylocytus TDH induces a calcium-dependent ion influx pathway that is not selective for Ca2+ and triggers a calcium-dependent Cl- secretion.
TDH induces a calcium influx in human and rat intestinal cells, which in turn triggers a chloride secretion, and at high concentrations, the toxin induces a calcium-independent cell death.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the mechanisms of TDH-induced enterotoxicity and cell death.
the elucidation of the mechanisms underlying the TDH-induced enterotoxicity and cytotoxicity and provides evidence for a correlation between these two effects.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanism of action of TDH.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hemolysins of V. parahemolyticus are able to induce both enterotoxic and cytolytic effects in intestinal cells.
TDH induces a calcium-dependent chloride secretory effect in intestinal cells at low toxin concentrations, whereas high toxin doses cause cell death by a calcium-independent mechanism.
TDH is a calcium- and chloride-dependent enterotoxin at low concentrations and a calcium-independent cytotoxin at high concentrations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the TDH has both enterotoxic and cytolytic activities, the latter being calcium independent.
TDH is a potent enterotoxin and cytotoxin.
TDH is a calcium-activated chloride channel and a cytotoxic protein.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TDH is a multifaceted toxin, with enterotoxic and cytolytic properties.
the hemolysinin is able to induce both enterotoxic and cytolytic effects on intestinal cells, and these two effects are interrelated in a dose-dependent manner.
the cytotoxic effect of the TDH is a secondary consequence of the enterotoxic effect and is not a primary mechanism of cell damage.
